summary.text:
Table 5 is the most interesting benchmarking table we have read. Torbay's investment portfolio has a weighted average maturity of 1,119 days against 95 days for similar authorities and 11 days for all authorities — about twelve times the peer group. Its credit score is better than peers and its bail-in exposure far lower (37% against 62%). The return, 4.40%, is below the 4.69% of similar authorities.

Paragraph 5.8 explains the trade deliberately: peers use pooled funds, which yield more now but are volatile and "may be subject to revenue impacts from potential changes to accounting regulations". Torbay bought fixed-return bonds instead — £10m at 4.118%, 4.551% and 4.802%, and a government bond with 5,418 days to run. That is a considered bet on the IFRS 9 override not surviving, taken through instrument choice rather than through a reserve.

The borrowing side mirrors it: £335.0m of PWLB at 2.97% over 25 years, no new borrowing, nothing maturing inside two years. Our 103 loans tie to their figure and price about £106.1m below par today.

Two addresses published. MID-YEAR PAPER at 30 September 2025 — scope every figure.

officer.body:
Hi Paul,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the mid-year review that went to Audit Committee in October and Council in December, recognising your 2025/26 outturn will have moved things on. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A scope note and a cross-check. What we hold is the mid-year paper, so everything below is at 30 September 2025. We hold 103 PWLB loans for Torbay totalling £334,598,155 against the £335.0m in your Table 3 — so we are looking at the same book. Your Table 1 foots as well: CFR £437m less £14m of other debt liabilities is the £423m borrowing CFR, financed by £351m external and £72m internal.

We wrote because of Table 5, which is the most interesting benchmarking table we have read this year. Your portfolio's weighted average maturity is 1,119 days. Similar authorities sit at 95 days and all authorities at 11. That is roughly twelve times the peer group, and it comes with a better credit score than peers (3.95 and AA- against 4.55 and A+) and far lower bail-in exposure (37% against 62%). The return, 4.40% against 4.69%, is the price.

What makes it worth writing about is that your paragraph 5.8 explains the trade rather than apologising for it: peers use pooled funds for strategic investments, which yield more today but are more volatile and "may be subject to revenue impacts from potential changes to accounting regulations in the near future". So you bought fixed-return bonds instead — £10m at 4.118%, 4.551% and 4.802%, and a government bond with 5,418 days to run.

That is, in effect, a position on whether the IFRS 9 statutory override survives 2029, taken through instrument choice rather than through a reserve. We have now read a lot of councils on this and almost all of them take the other side: hold the pooled fund, carry a reserve against the override lapsing, and hope. Tamworth is £1.1m down on £7.9m of property funds. Wandsworth carries an £8m volatility reserve and has stopped adding to multi-asset funds for exactly the reason you give. Swale keeps £350k against the same risk. You are the only council we have read that has changed the instrument rather than the provision.

We have no view on which is right — that depends on where the override lands and on your own liquidity needs, and 1,119 days is a real constraint. What we would offer is that it is a genuinely unusual position, it is well reasoned in your paper, and it is the kind of thing that is easier to defend to members when you can see how the rest of the sector is placed. That cross-council picture is what we assemble.

On the borrowing side there is nothing to do and we are not suggesting otherwise. £335.0m of PWLB at 2.97% with 25 years to run, no new borrowing, nothing maturing inside two years, and a virtually all-fixed book with no interest rate exposure. On the DMO's premature repayment curve today it prices about £106.1m below par — 97 of the 103 loans. Standard caveats: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

Your £5m LOBO with no lender option until 2028 is comfortably the least urgent in our library. For context, we have picked up eight LOBO calls across seven councils in the last few months and every one was refused — Oldham published being offered 6.70% and 7.67%, Wolverhampton 6.19% to 6.26%. Worth having in the diary for 2028 rather than now.

One small note for whoever compiles next year's report. Three of your total rows do not weight to their components: Table 3's total rate and maturity print as 4.22% and 43 years where the three rows weight to about 3.02% and 25.8 years, and Table 4's total return prints as 4.73% where the six rows weight to 4.22% (Table 2 gives 4.51% for the same total). The component figures are all internally consistent — it looks like simple rather than weighted averaging on the total lines. We mention it only because the totals are the numbers most likely to be quoted.

On training, four fit Torbay. Gilts as treasury investment and Financial instruments for treasury (IFRS 9) go directly to the bond strategy. Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset) for the other side of the same argument and the £4.4m you do hold. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Mid-Year Review 2025/26, Audit Committee 29 October 2025 (position at 30 September 2025).
